verses.text: Festus therefore, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
Then the high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed him against Paul, and they begged him,
asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem; plotting to kill him on the way.
However Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly.
“Let them therefore”, said he, “that are in power among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
When he had stayed among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be brought.
When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove,
while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”
But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem, and be judged by me there concerning these things?”
But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well.

For if I have done wrong, and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea, and greeted Festus.
As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left a prisoner by Felix;
about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him.

To whom I answered that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction, before the accused has met the accusers face to face, and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
When therefore they had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat, and commanded the man to be brought.
Concerning whom, when the accusers stood up, they brought no charge of such things as I supposed;
but had certain questions against him about their own religion, and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters.
But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.”

So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.

Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man, about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he himself appealed to the emperor I determined to send him,
of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination, I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”

footnotes.content: Festus takes his office seriously, moving quickly from Caesarea to Jerusalem to understand the land and its concerns. Three days is a short window, yet already the pattern emerges: the gospel makes ripples wherever the church goes, and earthly rulers must reckon with it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest and his allies see an opening with a new governor. They haven't forgotten Paul, and they move fast to shape Festus's first impression. Yet they're asking a Roman judge to do what the Jewish courts cannot—a sign of their spiritual desperation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Murder dressed as justice. They want Paul on that road where they can finish what they started in Jerusalem. But the Lord's protection over His witness is as steady as their malice—they ask, unaware that God has already planned Paul's journey to Rome.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus, though pagan and unfamiliar with Paul, follows Roman justice: the prisoner stays secure at headquarters. God often preserves His people through the very structures that would oppose them, if we have eyes to see His providence at work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let them come down with me and accuse him there." Festus offers a fair hearing—let the accusers face the accused. It's common justice, yet it's also how the Lord works: truth doesn't hide in shadows; it stands in the light and asks to be heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten days later, Festus returns to Caesarea and takes his seat on the judgment bench—the official seat of Roman authority. Paul now faces not Jerusalem's fervor but Rome's cold, measured power. Each setting changes the battle, but the Lord stands with His servant in every one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews arrive with many accusations, yet they carry no proof. It's a picture I've seen in my years: malice is loud, but it's often hollow when brought to the light. Truth and lies look very different when they both must speak in the same room.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's defense is brief and true: he has wronged no law, no temple, no Caesar. A clear conscience is a fortress. Before earthly judges and heavenly witnesses alike, he speaks what he has lived—faith without compromise and without panic.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus, new to his post and eager to please, tries to arrange a trial in Jerusalem where the Jews hold sway. Even a judge's kindness can become a trap if we let fear of men override God's calling. Paul sees what Festus cannot: this offer is a snare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am standing before Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be tried." Paul speaks with quiet authority. He knows the law, yes—but he also knows the Lord has sent him to Rome, not back to Jerusalem's scheming. Obedience sometimes means standing firm when others offer a gentler path.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's words are both submission and appeal: "If guilty, I don't refuse to die." Yet he knows he's innocent, and no innocent man should be handed over to false accusers. In that clarity, he invokes Caesar—not from cowardice, but from faith that God's purposes stand firm no matter who judges him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The appeal is granted: Paul will go to Caesar. Festus consults his council and confirms what Paul has invoked. In that moment, a fisherman from Galilee steps onto a path that will carry him to the heart of the empire itself. The Lord is never surprised by our circumstances.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: King Agrippa and his sister Bernice arrive at Caesarea—powerful figures, descended from the Herods, accustomed to favor and deference. Yet they come to hear the case of a prisoner, unaware that they're about to hear the gospel from a man who has surrendered everything to follow Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus lays the whole case before Agrippa—a prisoner left in custody, with charges the governor cannot quite understand. It's the moment when confusion opens a door. Sometimes the Lord works through our puzzlement when we're honest enough to admit we don't have all the answers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The chief priests and elders had sought a judgment against Paul—a sentence, not a trial. They wanted condemnation handed down, not justice discovered. How often we come to others seeking only confirmation of what we've already decided, forgetting that true justice requires an open ear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus states Roman law plainly: no one is condemned without facing his accusers and having a chance to defend himself. This principle—basic fairness, the right to be heard—is woven into the fabric of how God governs justice. Even pagan empires stumble toward truth sometimes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the accusers come together, Festus doesn't delay. He sits on the judgment seat and commands Paul brought forward. There's no cruelty here, no favoritism—only procedure. Sometimes the Lord preserves us through nothing more than a judge who does his duty fairly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the accusers stand, they bring no charges of wrongdoing—not against Jewish law, not against Caesar, nothing that Roman justice recognizes. Festus sees through the mask immediately. Truth has a shape; lies, when exposed, suddenly look naked.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Only religious questions remain, about Jesus and whether He rose from the dead. To Festus, this is a matter of Jewish superstition—but he hears it clearly: Paul affirms that Jesus lives. The gospel's central claim stands openly, declared before judges and witnesses, in the very court that would condemn it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus is perplexed about these religious matters. It's honest—he doesn't know what to make of a God who defeats death. So he asks Paul: "Would you go to Jerusalem and be tried there?" A pagan governor, baffled but fair, groping for an answer to a question that requires faith to understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul has already chosen his path: Caesar's judgment. Festus obeys, committing to send Paul to Rome with a full record. In that commitment, the prison door opens toward an empire, and the gospel is carried by a prisoner's chains to the very seat of earthly power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Agrippa—a king who knows the Jewish scriptures and customs—says, "I also would like to hear the man myself." Festus promises: "Tomorrow you shall hear him." Two powerful figures arrange to listen to a prisoner. Little do they know they're being drawn into God's design to showcase His gospel before the highest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next day unfolds with great pomp—Agrippa and Bernice, officers, chief men of the city, all arrayed in majesty. Then Paul is brought in. The contrast is stark: one prisoner, standing before crowns and authority. Yet he carries a power they cannot see, and his words will echo farther than their thrones ever reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus recounts the Jewish petition: they cry that Paul should die. He lays out the charge plainly before Agrippa, as if to say, "Here is the condemned man they demand—what do you make of him?" The truth is about to be spoken; the jury is about to hear it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus testifies: "He has committed nothing worthy of death." Here stands a Roman judge, examined Paul's case fairly, and found no guilt. Even in the eyes of unbelief, when justice is pursued honestly, the innocence of Christ's servants becomes plain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus confesses his perplexity: he has no clear charge to send to Caesar. So he's brought Paul before Agrippa, hoping the king's knowledge of Jewish matters will illuminate what the governor cannot grasp. Sometimes the Lord works through our honest confusion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It seems unreasonable to send a prisoner without specifying the charges." Festus seeks clarity and fairness, even as he sends Paul to Caesar. Readers today hear an echo in this: the gospel refuses to hide. It asks to be named, examined, judged by the light of truth. So it stands today—not in shadows, but open to scrutiny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
